records.prompt: Describe what it feels like to run across a pool of oobleck, a cornstarch-and-water mixture that firms up under each pounding step but swallows you if you stand still.

Explain why a dry stick of spaghetti bent from both ends almost never breaks into just two pieces, a puzzle that once intrigued Richard Feynman, and how twisting it first finally makes it snap cleanly in two.

Describe the moment in Seoul in 2016 when AlphaGo played its now-famous 'Move 37' against Lee Sedol, capturing how commentators first took it for a blunder before realizing they had witnessed a move no human would have dared to play.
Write a lyrical description of the Pythagorean idea of the music of the spheres, in which the planets hum in mathematical harmonies so constant that human ears have never noticed them.

Write a vivid reconstruction of the last day of Ötzi the Iceman, the 5,300-year-old man found in an Alpine glacier, drawing on clues from his final meal, his copper axe, his unfinished arrows and the arrowhead lodged in his shoulder.
Explain how a siphon lifts liquid up and over an obstacle, and why physicists still argue over whether gravity or atmospheric pressure deserves the credit.
Write a brief story in which a hiker in a remote Australian canyon stumbles upon a grove of trees that were thought to have vanished alongside the dinosaurs.

Explain the hydraulic jump, the circular ring that forms where water from a tap spreads across the bottom of a sink and suddenly thickens, and how it relates to the tidal bores that surge up great rivers.

Explain Cantor's diagonal argument and why it proves there are more real numbers than whole numbers, walking the reader through the trick of building a number that differs from every entry on any supposedly complete list.

Write a passage explaining why ancient Roman concrete has survived two thousand years in harbors and domes while modern concrete cracks within decades, including the discovery of lime clasts that let it heal its own cracks.

Explain how planets grow from microscopic grains of dust in a young star's disk, including the puzzling 'metre-size barrier' at which growing pebbles should spiral into the star before they can become planets.
Argue whether laws against price gouging after natural disasters protect vulnerable people or end up worsening shortages by blunting the price signals that draw supplies into stricken areas.

Take a position on Ada Lovelace's famous objection that the Analytical Engine can only do whatever we know how to order it to perform, and argue whether today's AI systems have proved her right or wrong.
Explain the surprisingly unsettled science of why ice is slippery, and why the old textbook story that a skate blade melts the ice by pressure does not hold up.
Explain how a date palm seed recovered from the ruins of Masada, roughly two thousand years old, was coaxed into germinating, and what that reveals about seed dormancy.

Describe the night during the siege of Constantinople in 1453 when Ottoman soldiers hauled dozens of warships over a hill on greased wooden rails to slip past the great chain guarding the Golden Horn.
Explain phage therapy, the century-old idea of using viruses that infect only bacteria to cure infections, and why it is being revived as antibiotics fail.

Explain John Locke's experiment of warming one hand and chilling the other before plunging both into the same lukewarm water, and how it supports his distinction between primary and secondary qualities.

Write a tender description of a kitchen doorframe marked with pencil lines and dates recording children's heights over many years, as seen on the day the family carries out the last box and moves away.

Argue whether the 'Hubble tension,' the stubborn disagreement between different measurements of how fast the universe is expanding, is more likely to signal new physics or an undiscovered measurement error.

Write a lyrical description of a bowl of fruit on a kitchen table over the course of one week as it ripens, softens and finally decays, in the spirit of a seventeenth-century Dutch vanitas still life.
Explain why the viral 2015 photograph of 'the dress' split viewers between blue-and-black and white-and-gold, focusing on the brain's unconscious assumptions about lighting and color constancy.
Describe the forests and abandoned streets of the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone today, where wolves, wild horses and bison roam in the absence of people.
Write a vivid passage about the great Leonid meteor storm of November 1833, when tens of thousands of shooting stars an hour woke and frightened people across North America.
Explain Harry Frankfurt's distinction between a liar and a bullshitter, and why he thought indifference to the truth is more corrosive than deliberately denying it.
Describe what it would be like to be Ireneo Funes from Borges' story, a man who forgets nothing and is therefore barely able to think, because thinking requires forgetting differences.
Argue whether an artificial intelligence that behaved in every way as if it suffered would deserve moral consideration, even if we could never be sure it felt anything.
Write a story in which a 1920s light-bulb engineer is ordered by the Phoebus cartel to make bulbs that burn out after 1,000 hours, and must wrestle with designing failure into his own invention.
Explain how cuttlefish change color and skin texture in a fraction of a second to blend into their surroundings, even though they appear to be color-blind.

Explain how the Comte de Buffon showed that randomly dropping needles onto a floor of parallel boards can be used to estimate the value of pi, and why a circle's constant turns up in a problem about straight lines.
Explain generative adversarial networks through the image of an art forger and a detective locked in an escalating contest, each improving only because the other keeps getting better.

Write a short reflective passage about the screeching, warbling handshake of a dial-up modem, evoking both the nostalgia of the sound and what the two machines were actually negotiating as they 'sang' to each other.

Explain the philosophical argument of Dostoevsky's parable of the Grand Inquisitor, who tells a returned Christ that humanity cannot bear the burden of freedom and longs instead for bread, miracle, mystery and authority.
Explain what brown dwarfs are, objects too massive to be planets but too small to sustain hydrogen fusion, and why they are often called 'failed stars.'
Write a short reflective passage about the Hubble Deep Field, in which astronomers aimed the telescope for days at a seemingly empty speck of sky and found it crowded with thousands of galaxies.

Explain why the harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + ... grows without limit despite its ever-shrinking terms, and how this lets you stack identical books at the edge of a table so the top one overhangs as far as you like.

Explain the problem facing the designers of Finland's Onkalo nuclear waste repository: how to warn people a hundred thousand years from now, who may share none of our languages or symbols, never to dig there.
Write a lyrical description of a total lunar eclipse, conveying that the Moon's copper-red glow is the light of every sunrise and sunset on Earth at once.

Explain to a curious teenager how zero grew from a humble placeholder dot into a true number with its own rules in the work of the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta, and why 'nothing' turned out to be one of humanity's greatest ideas.

Explain the central limit theorem through an everyday analogy, showing why adding up many small, independent random nudges so reliably produces the familiar bell-shaped curve, whatever the nudges look like individually.

Describe a bustling medieval trade fair in the Champagne region of France, where merchants from Italy and Flanders met to trade cloth, spices and written promises of payment, giving birth to early forms of credit.
Explain the puzzle of the 'Methuselah star' HD 140283, whose age was first estimated to be greater than that of the universe itself, and how astronomers resolved the apparent contradiction.

Describe what it would be like to free dive into deep blue water on a single breath, as the mammalian dive reflex slows the heart, the light from the surface fades and the body begins to sink without effort.
Using the analogy of a car's speedometer and odometer, explain the fundamental theorem of calculus and why the slope of a curve and the area beneath it turn out to be two sides of the same coin.
Write a reflective passage about how tuberculosis, known as consumption, was romanticized in the nineteenth century as a disease of poets and artists, before the bacterium behind it was identified.
Explain the holographic principle, the idea that all the information inside a region of space might be encoded on its boundary, like a three-dimensional image stored on a flat hologram.
Compare chimpanzees and bonobos, our two closest living relatives, in how they resolve conflict and organize their societies, and reflect on what each suggests about human nature.
Argue whether the Y2K millennium bug was an overblown panic or a genuine disaster quietly averted by years of unglamorous work by programmers.
Describe the journey of a single red blood cell as it squeezes through capillaries, picks up oxygen in the lungs and returns to the heart, written as a vivid travelogue.
Argue whether Socrates was right that the unexamined life is not worth living, or whether a life of unreflective contentment can be just as good.
Explain the optimal stopping strategy known as the secretary problem, or the 37 percent rule, and half-seriously apply it to someone trying to decide when to stop viewing apartments and sign a lease.

Write an engaging explanation of how MP3 compression shrinks music by discarding sounds the human ear cannot perceive, such as quiet tones masked by louder ones close in pitch, so that most of the data vanishes without listeners noticing.

Describe Tenochtitlan as Spanish soldiers first saw it in 1519, an island city of causeways, canals, floating chinampa gardens and gleaming temples rising from Lake Texcoco, which some of them compared to an enchanted vision from a romance.

Write a short reflective passage imagining Antonie van Leeuwenhoek's astonishment as he peered through his tiny handmade lens at a drop of rainwater and became the first person ever to see it teeming with living 'animalcules'.
Argue whether the last person alive on Earth would be doing anything wrong by destroying a forest on their final day, and what the answer reveals about whether nature has value in itself.

Explain Kolmogorov complexity, the idea that the true information content of something is the length of the shortest program that could produce it, opening with the question of whether a million zeros or a million random coin flips is more 'complex.'

Describe what it would be like to climb the narrow stairs between the two shells of Brunelleschi's dome in Florence, seeing up close the herringbone brickwork that let the largest masonry dome in the world rise without wooden scaffolding beneath it.
Explain why the far side of the Moon is not actually dark, and why its rugged, crater-packed face looks so different from the familiar near side.

Explain how thousands of fireflies in the Great Smoky Mountains come to flash in near-perfect unison each June with no conductor directing them, in a passage that reads like the description of an orchestra tuning itself in the dark.
Explain how Giuseppe Peano constructed a continuous curve that passes through every single point of a square, and why such a 'monster' unsettled mathematicians' intuitions about what dimension means.
Explain how a handclap at the foot of the stepped pyramid of El Castillo at Chichén Itzá returns as a descending chirp that some have likened to the call of the sacred quetzal bird.
Describe the Laetoli footprints, left about 3.6 million years ago by upright-walking hominins crossing fresh volcanic ash in what is now Tanzania, imagining the moment they were made.

Explain the scientific quarrel between Luigi Galvani and Alessandro Volta over why dissected frog legs twitched when touched with metal, and how their dispute gave the world both the electric battery and the study of nerve signals.

Using the metaphor of a nervous system stretched across a continent, explain how the Mongol Empire's Yam network of relay stations, fresh horses and riders carried messages across Eurasia at astonishing speed, and how a metal tablet called a paiza served as a traveler's passport.
Argue whether learning to cook food over fire was the decisive step that made us human, as the cooking hypothesis proposes.
Explain the theory that Viking navigators used 'sunstones,' crystals of Iceland spar, to find the Sun's position through clouds by detecting the polarization of skylight.

Write a reflective passage on Pascal's claim that humanity's troubles stem from our inability to sit quietly alone in a room, imagining what a person is fleeing from each time they reach for a diversion.

Explain fully homomorphic encryption using the metaphor of a locked glovebox in which a jeweler can craft a ring without ever touching or seeing the gold, just as a cloud server can compute on data it can never read.
Explain Newton's rotating bucket argument and why the curved surface of spinning water puzzled thinkers from Newton to Ernst Mach to Einstein about what rotation is really relative to.

Describe, in vivid prose, what an observer sees when liquid helium is cooled to about two degrees above absolute zero and suddenly stops boiling, then begins creeping up and over the walls of its container as a frictionless superfluid.
Argue for or against the 'block universe' view, which holds that past, present and future are equally real and that the flowing 'now' we experience is an illusion.
Explain why a tsunami can cross the deep ocean as fast as a jet airliner while being barely noticeable to ships, and why it rears up into a towering wall only as it reaches shallow coastal water.
Write a short reflective passage about Heinrich Hertz's remark that the electromagnetic waves he had just produced in his laboratory were of no use whatsoever.
Explain how the 'immortal jellyfish' Turritopsis dohrnii can revert from its adult form to a juvenile stage when stressed, potentially repeating its life cycle indefinitely.
Describe what it would be like to lose your sense of proprioception overnight, so that you could only know where your limbs were by looking at them.
Write a lyrical description of the zodiacal light, the faint, tilted cone of glow that rises from the horizon before dawn, made by sunlight scattering off dust between the planets.
Explain how a Bornean pitcher plant has evolved to serve as a toilet for tree shrews, collecting their droppings as fertilizer rather than relying on trapped insects.

Describe the discovery of the first pulsar in 1967, when a graduate student noticed a bit of 'scruff' on a long strip of chart paper, a signal so regular it was half-jokingly labelled LGM-1, for 'little green men.'
Explain how a solitary desert grasshopper transforms into a gregarious swarming locust when crowded, changing its color, its behaviour and even the size of its brain.
Argue whether the dead can be wronged, for example by breaking a deathbed promise or slandering someone long after they are gone, even though they will never know.

Explain Clark and Chalmers' extended mind thesis through the story of Otto, a man with memory loss who relies on a notebook to find his way to a museum, and whether that notebook is literally part of his mind.

Explain how Cecilia Payne, in her 1925 doctoral thesis, showed that stars are made overwhelmingly of hydrogen and helium, a conclusion so contrary to accepted belief that she was persuaded to call it 'almost certainly not real.'

Write a short, mind-bending piece explaining Thomson's lamp, a lamp switched on and off infinitely many times within two minutes, and why asking whether it is on or off at the end exposes deep puzzles about completing infinite tasks.
Write an evocative passage describing the autumn of 1918, when a new strain of influenza swept the world and struck down healthy young adults with frightening speed.
Explain Aristotle's puzzle about tomorrow's sea battle: if it is already true today that a battle will happen tomorrow, does that make the future fixed and our deliberation pointless?

Explain the Kepler conjecture about the densest way to stack cannonballs, and why a fact every greengrocer piling oranges already seemed to know took nearly four centuries and a massive computer-assisted proof to settle.
Write a playful, reflective passage about the experience of an earworm, a song fragment that loops endlessly in the mind, weaving in what is known about why certain tunes get stuck.

Describe the atmosphere of the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels, where Einstein would arrive at breakfast with a new thought experiment to undermine quantum theory and Bohr would have a rebuttal ready by dinner.
Write a lyrical description of the swirling colours on a soap bubble, explaining how they arise from light interfering within a film thinner than a wavelength.

Describe the scene Sartre imagines of a person peering through a keyhole, utterly absorbed, who suddenly hears footsteps in the hall and is flooded with shame at being seen, as an illustration of how the gaze of others shapes who we are.
Write a brief story about the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa from the Louvre, told from the perspective of the handyman who walked out of the museum with the painting hidden under his smock.
Write a reflective passage about the ginkgo trees that survived the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and still grow there, remembering that ginkgos as a lineage have outlasted the dinosaurs.

Describe the predawn moment of the Trinity test in the New Mexico desert in July 1945, conveying the impossible light, the wave of heat, the delayed thunder and the uneasy silence among the scientists who watched.

Explain how Claude Chappe's optical telegraph, a chain of hilltop towers with pivoting wooden arms, could carry messages across revolutionary France in minutes, half a century before the electric telegraph.
Explain the hairy ball theorem—why you can never comb a hairy coconut flat without leaving a cowlick—and why it guarantees that somewhere on Earth the wind is not blowing at all.

Explain how the young Leonhard Euler solved the Basel problem, showing that the sum of the reciprocals of the square numbers equals π²/6, and why finding pi in a problem with no circles in sight caused such a sensation.

Write a short reflective passage imagining Marcus Aurelius writing his private Meditations by lamplight in a cold military camp on the Danube frontier, the most powerful man in the world reminding himself to be humble, patient and kind.

Write a reflective passage about Point Nemo, the oceanic pole of inaccessibility so remote that the nearest humans are often astronauts passing overhead, and where retired spacecraft are sent to sink.

Write a brief story in which swift Achilles races a tortoise that has been given a head start and slowly realizes, as Zeno argued, that each time he reaches where the tortoise was, it has crept a little further ahead.

Explain the decoy effect using the magazine subscription experiment in which adding an unattractive print-only option, priced the same as print plus web, dramatically shifted buyers toward the combined deal.

Write an evocative passage on Kierkegaard's claim that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom, using the image of someone at the edge of a cliff who feels not only the fear of falling but the terrifying possibility of jumping.

Write a calm, meditative passage explaining the Japanese practice of shinrin-yoku, or 'forest bathing', and the research suggesting that unhurried time among trees can lower stress hormones, heart rate and blood pressure.
Explain gamma-ray bursts, the most luminous explosions in the universe, and the irony that they were first detected by satellites built to watch for secret nuclear weapons tests.
Write a brief story in which a volunteer astronomer in 1977, poring over computer printouts from the Big Ear radio telescope, circles a strange sequence of characters and writes 'Wow!' in the margin.
Explain the placebo effect, including the surprising findings that larger pills, pricier pills and even placebos given openly as placebos can produce measurable relief.
Describe Plato's allegory from the Phaedrus of the soul as a charioteer driving two winged horses, one noble and one unruly, in vivid, dramatic prose.
Argue whether the legend that Archimedes set Roman warships ablaze with mirrors during the siege of Syracuse could have been physically possible.

Write a lyrical description of Great Zimbabwe at its height in the fourteenth century, imagining the sweeping granite walls of the Great Enclosure and the traders arriving with gold, ivory and Chinese porcelain.
Explain the counterintuitive rule of orbital mechanics that to catch up with a spacecraft ahead of you in the same orbit, you must first fire your engines backwards and slow down.

Argue for or against G.H. Hardy's proud claim that the purest mathematics is valuable precisely because it is useless, considering that his beloved number theory later became a backbone of internet security.
Explain the 'windshield phenomenon,' the observation that car windshields no longer get splattered with insects as they did decades ago, and what scientists have found about the decline of insects.
Argue whether Brutalist architecture, with its massive forms of raw concrete, is an ugly relic that should be demolished or an honest and heroic style worth preserving.
Take a position on whether photographing every beautiful moment on a phone diminishes our ability to truly experience and remember it, and defend that position with feeling.

Explain the idea that dopamine signals not pleasure itself but the gap between expected and actual reward, illustrated by the monkey experiments in which neurons came to fire at a predictive light rather than at the juice.

Write a meditative description of a Turing machine at work, its reading head inching back and forth along an endless paper tape one symbol at a time, and yet capable in principle of any computation a modern supercomputer can perform.

Explain how a gravity assist works, showing how a spacecraft can steal a little of a planet's orbital momentum to speed up, using the image of a tennis ball bouncing off the front of an oncoming train.

Explain William Paley's watchmaker argument, which begins with stumbling upon a watch lying on a heath, and how Darwin's theory of natural selection offered a way to get design-like order without a designer.
In a light, reassuring tone, explain the friendship paradox—why, on average, your friends have more friends than you do—to someone who suspects everyone else is simply more popular.
Explain how metamaterials, engineered structures with properties not found in nature, can steer light around an object and make invisibility cloaks a real, if limited, possibility.
Describe the Philae lander's improbable touchdown on comet 67P in 2014, bouncing twice across the surface in the comet's feeble gravity before coming to rest in shadow beside a cliff.
Explain why we still divide hours into sixty minutes and circles into 360 degrees, tracing these habits back to the Babylonian base-60 number system and the practical advantages that made it endure.
Explain why the tritone earned the nickname 'diabolus in musica', what makes this interval sound so restless and unresolved, and how it later became essential to blues, jazz and heavy metal.
Explain why flashbulb memories of shocking public events feel vividly certain yet drift dramatically over the years, as studies of people's recollections of the Challenger disaster revealed.

Explain differential privacy for a reader who has never written a line of code, showing how adding carefully calibrated random noise to statistics lets a census learn about a population without revealing anything about any single person in it.
Write a brief story about a crow who remembers the face of a person who once trapped it and, years later, leads its whole family to scold that person in the street.
Write a brief story set centuries in the future, in which a child plants a seed retrieved from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault and grows a crop that no one alive has ever tasted.
Explain al-Ghazali's example of cotton brought into contact with fire, and his argument that we never actually observe the fire causing the burning, only one event regularly accompanying another.
Explain how bee orchids deceive male bees by mimicking the look, feel and scent of a female, tricking them into carrying pollen without offering any reward.

Write a lyrical description of how an AI diffusion model creates a picture, starting from pure television static and removing noise step by step until a recognizable scene emerges, like a photograph slowly developing in a darkroom tray.

Argue whether a person who was as morally good as possible in every action would be someone to admire, or whether, as Susan Wolf suggested, such a moral saint would lack something essential to a good life.

Write a vivid scene describing the day in 1947 when operators of the Harvard Mark II computer found a moth trapped in one of its relays and taped it into the logbook as the 'first actual case of bug being found.'

Explain how thousands of starlings in a murmuration move as a single rippling shape without any leader, each bird responding only to its nearest handful of neighbours, in prose that captures the wonder of watching it over a marsh at dusk.

Explain how high-energy particles from space can flip a single bit inside a computer's memory, referencing the 2003 Belgian election in which one candidate inexplicably gained exactly 4,096 extra votes, and how engineers guard against such invisible strikes.
Explain why Earth has seasons, gently correcting the widespread belief that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.
Describe how, in 1932, Bell Labs engineer Karl Jansky, hunting for sources of static that troubled transatlantic telephone calls, found a faint hiss coming from the center of the Milky Way.
Explain the puzzle of Buridan's ass, the perfectly rational donkey that starves between two identical bales of hay, and what it reveals about choosing when reasons are perfectly balanced.

Write a lyrical description of walking through Pando in Utah, a grove of tens of thousands of quaking aspens that are all one organism sharing a single ancient root system, while its leaves tremble gold in the autumn wind.

Explain digital steganography, the art of hiding a secret message inside an ordinary-looking photograph by subtly altering the least significant bits of its pixels, and how its goal differs from that of encryption.
Write a reflective passage about Pando, the grove of quaking aspen in Utah that is actually a single organism with tens of thousands of trunks sharing one root system.

Explain the 'Great Dimming' of Betelgeuse in 2019–2020, when the red supergiant faded noticeably and fuelled speculation that it was about to explode, and what astronomers concluded had actually happened.

Explain how Henrietta Swan Leavitt, working as a poorly paid human 'computer' at Harvard Observatory, discovered that the pulsing rhythm of certain stars reveals their true brightness, giving astronomers their first yardstick for measuring the universe.

Explain the geological theory that the trances of the Pythia, the priestess of the Oracle at Delphi, were induced by sweet-smelling gases rising from fault lines beneath Apollo's temple, and why the idea is still debated.

Explain why looking up at the night sky is really looking into the past, since the light reaching your eyes from some stars set out before your great-grandparents were born, in a tone of quiet astonishment.
Describe what happens inside a chrysalis as a caterpillar dissolves much of its body into a soup of cells and rebuilds itself as a butterfly.

Write an explanatory passage about hemispatial neglect, the condition in which a stroke patient may eat only the right half of their plate and draw clocks with all twelve numbers crowded onto one side.
Explain how the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann, studying faint seismic waves from a 1929 earthquake, deduced in 1936 that Earth has a solid inner core hidden within its liquid outer core.

Explain how the first message sent over ARPANET in October 1969 was supposed to read 'LOGIN' but crashed the system after two letters, and how the idea of packet switching made the network that grew into the internet possible.

Explain how group theory describes the Rubik's Cube and how mathematicians proved that every one of its 43 quintillion scrambled positions can be solved in twenty moves or fewer, a figure nicknamed 'God's number.'

Explain the Gale–Shapley stable matching algorithm, why it always produces pairings in which no two people would both rather abandon their partners for each other, and how a version of it now matches new doctors to hospitals.
Explain the incongruity theory of humor, associated with thinkers like Kant and Schopenhauer, showing how laughter springs from the sudden collapse of an expectation into something absurd.
Explain the phenomenon of ant mills, in which army ants blindly following pheromone trails can become trapped in a circling death spiral, and what it reveals about the limits of simple rules.
Explain the Stoic dichotomy of control as taught by Epictetus, a philosopher who had once been enslaved, and how separating what is up to us from what is not was meant to make a person unshakable.
Write a short reflective passage about kintsugi, the Japanese art of mending broken pottery with gold-dusted lacquer, using it as a metaphor for how people carry their own repaired fractures.
Describe, in the second person, standing on a misty mountain ridge with the Sun at your back and seeing your own giant shadow cast on the clouds, ringed by a rainbow halo called a glory.
Describe what it would be like to climb Olympus Mons on Mars, a volcano so vast and gently sloped that its summit would lie beyond the horizon for someone standing at its base.
Explain who 'Mitochondrial Eve' was and why she was neither the first woman nor the only woman alive in her time.
Describe what it would be like to perceive the world through echolocation as a bat, hunting moths in the dark by listening to the shapes of returning echoes.

Explain Hannah Arendt's phrase 'the banality of evil,' coined while she observed the trial of Adolf Eichmann, and why her suggestion that great harm can flow from thoughtless obedience unsettled so many readers.
Write a lyrical monologue in the voice of an old manual typewriter gathering dust in an attic, which remembers every love letter, unfinished novel and rejection notice it ever struck onto paper.
Explain why comets often show two distinct tails, one of dust and one of ions, and why both point away from the Sun even when the comet is heading outward.
Explain to a curious ten-year-old why you get a little electric shock when you touch a doorknob after shuffling across a carpet, especially on dry winter days.
Write an evocative passage imagining the night before twenty-year-old Évariste Galois's fatal duel in 1832, as he hurriedly scrawled his mathematical ideas into a final letter to a friend.
Describe the moment in 1923 when Edwin Hubble, studying a photographic plate of the Andromeda 'nebula,' crossed out an 'N' and scrawled 'VAR!', realizing it was a whole galaxy far beyond our own.
Describe what Earth might have looked like during a Snowball Earth episode, when ice may have reached nearly to the equator and life clung on in hidden refuges.
Describe Welwitschia mirabilis in the Namib Desert, a plant that grows only two leaves in its entire life of a thousand years or more, letting them fray into ribbons across the sand.

Explain why Jeremy Bentham insisted that the question about animals is not whether they can reason or talk but whether they can suffer, and how this reframing reshaped moral thinking about other species.

Explain what scientists currently understand about how general anesthesia switches off consciousness, and why it remains remarkable that doctors can reliably make a mind vanish and return without fully knowing how.
Describe the eerie blue-violet glow of St. Elmo's fire crackling on the masts of a sailing ship during a storm, and the physics of electrical discharge behind it.
Write a short story about Johannes Kepler's years-long 'war with Mars,' ending at the moment he realizes the planet's orbit is not a circle but an ellipse.
Explain Braess's paradox, in which adding a new road to a network can make every driver's journey slower, and describe how closing roads in some real cities has actually eased congestion.

Explain Maxwell's demon as if introducing a mischievous character in a fable, describing the tiny being that sorts fast and slow molecules to seemingly defeat the second law of thermodynamics, and why erasing its memory ultimately foils it.

Write a playful description of a troupe of folk dancers performing a bubble sort, swapping places pair by pair until the line stands in perfect numerical order, conveying both the charm and the comic inefficiency of the algorithm.

Describe the Christmas Truce of 1914, when British and German soldiers along the Western Front climbed out of their frozen trenches to sing carols, trade cigarettes and kick a football across no man's land.

Explain reward hacking, or specification gaming, in reinforcement learning, using the famous example of an AI boat-racing agent that learned to spin in endless circles collecting points instead of ever finishing the race.

Argue whether the 1989 cold fusion announcement, in which two chemists claimed to have produced nuclear fusion in a tabletop cell, should be remembered as an embarrassment for science or as proof that its self-correcting machinery works.

Write a lyrical description of Machu Picchu at dawn as the clouds lift from the surrounding peaks, lingering on the Inca stone walls fitted together so precisely, without mortar, that not even a knife blade can slip between them.
Argue whether Albert Einstein deserves the lion's share of credit for special relativity, given that Hendrik Lorentz and Henri Poincaré had already worked out much of its mathematics.
Explain how stromatolites, layered mounds built by microbial mats, preserve some of the oldest evidence of life on Earth and still grow today in Shark Bay, Australia.
Write a calm, reflective passage on Lucretius' symmetry argument: since we feel no distress at the eternity that passed before we were born, why should we fear the eternity that follows our death?

Explain the Michelson–Morley experiment of 1887, which searched for the 'aether wind' through which light was supposed to travel, and why its null result is often called the most important failed experiment in physics.

Explain the quantum Zeno effect, the strange prediction, since confirmed in the laboratory, that repeatedly observing an unstable quantum system can freeze it in place, like a watched pot that truly never boils.
Explain what a white hole is, the time-reversed twin of a black hole that nothing can ever enter, and why physicists debate whether such objects could exist in nature.

Describe how Christiaan Huygens, sick in bed in 1665, noticed that two pendulum clocks hanging from the same beam had mysteriously fallen into step with each other, which he called an 'odd kind of sympathy.'

Write a lyrical description, opening with the words 'Every ruin was once someone's present,' of the strange pleasure people have long taken in ruins, from ivy on broken arches to roofless abbeys open to the sky.
Explain how a falling cat manages to turn itself over and land on its feet with nothing to push against, a puzzle that once seemed to defy the conservation of angular momentum.

Explain what historians know and still debate about Greek fire, the Byzantine weapon that kept burning even on water, and how its formula was guarded so jealously that it was eventually lost to history.

Describe what it feels like to experience the rubber hand illusion, when a fake hand stroked in sync with your hidden real one suddenly feels like your own, and what it reveals about how fragile our sense of the body is.
Explain why scratching an itch feels so satisfying, including how the mild pain of scratching temporarily silences itch signals in the spinal cord.
Describe the day Vesuvius erupted in 79 CE through the eyes of a Pompeii baker sliding the morning's loaves into his oven as a strange, pine-shaped cloud begins to rise over the mountain.

Explain what it would mean for pi to be a 'normal' number, and why, despite trillions of computed digits, nobody can yet prove that every finite string of digits, such as your phone number, must appear somewhere in its expansion.
Describe, from the perspective of the prisoner in Plato's cave who is dragged up into the sunlight, the pain, confusion and slow wonder of seeing real things for the first time.
Explain why certain moments in music can send a shiver down the spine, exploring what happens in the brain's reward system during musical frisson.
Write a lyrical description of the date-due slip glued inside an old library book, its column of stamped dates stretching back decades, imagining the strangers who each carried the same story home.
Explain how ultramarine, the luminous blue pigment ground from Afghan lapis lazuli, came to cost more than gold in Renaissance Europe, and why painters reserved it for the robes of the Virgin Mary.
Explain how about two meters of DNA is packed into a cell nucleus only a few millionths of a meter across, using the analogy of thread wound onto spools.
Argue against the persistent myth that old cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is a slowly flowing liquid, making the case for what glass really is.
Write a brief story retelling Archimedes' 'Eureka!' moment, in which a king's suspicion about a golden crown leads him to the principle of buoyancy in the public baths.
Explain how the fourth-century Roman Lycurgus Cup glows jade green in reflected light but blood red when lit from within, and how its glassmakers unknowingly practiced a kind of nanotechnology.

Write a vivid sensory description of a Phoenician dye works in ancient Tyre, where heaps of crushed murex sea snails rotted in vats to produce the foul-smelling but priceless purple worn by kings and emperors.
Argue whether the Western Roman Empire truly 'fell' in 476 CE, or whether it is more accurate to say it gradually transformed into the kingdoms of early medieval Europe.
Compare the correspondence and coherence theories of truth, using the image of a map judged either by how well it matches the land or by how consistently it fits with all the other maps we trust.

Write a lyrical description of a neural network learning, imagining training as a blindfolded traveler descending a vast mountain range at night, feeling for the slope underfoot in search of a valley of low error.
Explain why the titan arum, or corpse flower, heats itself up and smells of rotting flesh when it blooms, and which pollinators it is trying to fool.
Explain Wittgenstein's idea of family resemblance by asking what board games, ball games, card games and solitaire actually have in common, and why many of our concepts lack crisp definitions.
Describe the moment in 1963 when Stanisław Ulam, doodling through a dull lecture, wrote the whole numbers in a square spiral and saw the primes gather along mysterious diagonal lines.
Write a haunting, reflective passage about Kafka's parable of the man who waits his whole life before the open door of the Law, only to learn at the very end that the door was meant for him alone.

Explain the diamond-water paradox, why water, essential to life, is cheap while diamonds are expensive, and how the idea of marginal utility finally resolved the puzzle, as if speaking to someone holding a glass of water in one hand and a diamond ring in the other.

Argue whether a handwritten letter carries something that no email or text message ever can, considering the ink, the handwriting, the slowness of the post and the fact that it can sit in a drawer for fifty years.
Explain why killer whales are among the very few animals that go through menopause, and how post-reproductive grandmothers lead their pods to salmon in lean years.

Explain the Alcubierre warp drive, a solution of Einstein's equations in which a ship rides a bubble of contracted space ahead and expanded space behind, and the exotic obstacles that keep it in the realm of speculation.

Explain what a Bose–Einstein condensate is, using the image of a crowd of individual singers merging into one perfectly unified choir to describe how atoms cooled near absolute zero begin to behave as a single quantum wave.

Describe the twelve seconds of the Wright brothers' first powered flight on the cold, windy dunes near Kitty Hawk in December 1903, as seen by one of the handful of local men who happened to witness it.

Explain modular arithmetic using the face of a clock, showing how this wrap-around way of counting underlies everything from working out the day of the week to the check digit printed on a book's barcode.

Explain how the Monte Carlo method was born when Stanisław Ulam, convalescing from illness and playing solitaire, wondered whether he could estimate his odds of winning simply by playing many random games, and how the idea spread from there.

Explain to a frustrated commuter how Braess's paradox means that adding a new road to a congested network can make everyone's journey slower, and why removing a highway in Seoul did not cause traffic chaos.
Write a short story in which a reindeer herder in the Siberian taiga witnesses the Tunguska explosion on the morning of June 30, 1908.

Write a lyrical passage about the so-called 52-hertz whale, whose song is pitched higher than that of any known whale, imagining it calling across the Pacific for decades in a voice no other whale seems to answer.

Explain the grandfather paradox of time travel, imagining a traveler who journeys back to stop their grandparents from ever meeting, and the main escape routes proposed, from self-consistent timelines to branching universes.

Describe the long, drifting voyage of a message in a bottle tossed from a ship's deck, carried by ocean currents for decades before washing up on a distant beach to be read by someone not yet born when it was written.
Write a lyrical description of a whale fall, the slow, decades-long feast that unfolds on the seafloor after a whale's body sinks into the deep.
Explain loss aversion and Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, beginning with why most people refuse a coin flip that would win them $150 on heads but cost them $100 on tails.
Explain Keynes's 'beauty contest' analogy for financial markets, together with the 'guess two-thirds of the average' game that shows how investors end up trying to predict what others will predict.
Explain Robert Nozick's utility monster, a creature that gains vastly more pleasure from every resource than anyone else could, and why it is meant to embarrass simple versions of utilitarianism.

Explain Gauss's Theorema Egregium, his 'remarkable theorem' about curvature, using the trick of folding a floppy pizza slice into a U-shape so its tip doesn't droop, and show why it also means every flat map of the Earth must distort something.
Write a vivid description of the giant impact that likely formed the Moon, when a Mars-sized body known as Theia struck the young Earth and flung a ring of molten debris into orbit.
Explain the physics of quicksand, and why, contrary to what films suggest, a person stuck in it cannot actually sink all the way under.
Argue whether hope, the one thing left inside Pandora's jar, is humanity's greatest consolation or, as Nietzsche suggested, the worst of evils because it prolongs our torment.
Explain why absolute zero can be approached ever more closely but never actually reached, using the metaphor of a staircase whose steps keep getting smaller.
Describe an army ant bivouac, a living nest built from the interlocked bodies of hundreds of thousands of ants, and the raiding column that pours out of it at dawn.
Explain the concept of learned helplessness, how it was first discovered, and how later research reframed it as a failure to learn that we have control rather than a lesson in having none.
Explain the evidence that Saturn's rings may be geologically young and slowly raining down onto the planet, meaning we may happen to live in a brief era when Saturn wears them.

Explain how zero came to be treated as a number in its own right in India, with Brahmagupta setting down rules for calculating with it in the seventh century, and why this was such a profound conceptual leap.

Write a sober explanatory passage about the Therac-25 radiation therapy machine of the 1980s, explaining how a race condition triggered by fast-typing operators led to massive overdoses and why the case became a founding lesson in software safety.

Explain the mathematics of fair division, starting with the 'I cut, you choose' rule for two people and showing why dividing a cake so that none of three or more guests envies another is surprisingly tricky.

Explain the isoperimetric problem through the legend of Queen Dido, who was granted as much land as an ox-hide could enclose and cleverly cut it into a thin strip to encircle the hill that became Carthage.
Write a moving passage about Leonhard Euler's final years, when, nearly blind, he continued to pour out mathematics by dictating calculations he carried entirely in his head.
Explain Galileo's elegant thought experiment of tying a heavy stone to a light one, which shows by pure logic that Aristotle was wrong to claim heavier objects fall faster.
Describe the nonstop flight of a bar-tailed godwit from Alaska to New Zealand, more than eleven thousand kilometers over open ocean without landing, eating or drinking.
Explain the sunk cost fallacy using the Concorde supersonic airliner, which the British and French governments kept funding long after it was clear it would never pay for itself.

Take a side in the Sleeping Beauty problem—upon waking with no memory of any previous awakening, should she believe the coin landed heads with probability one half or one third?—and defend it against the opposing camp.
Explain the paradox of thrift, how saving more, sensible for any single household, can deepen a recession when everyone does it at once, using a small fishing village as the illustrative example.

Explain why ice floats, an oddity since most substances are denser as solids, and how that quirk lets lakes freeze from the top down so that fish survive the winter in the dim water beneath a roof of ice.
Explain the finding that beach evening primrose flowers sweeten their nectar within minutes of 'hearing' the wingbeats of a pollinating bee, with their petals acting like an ear.
Write a vivid description of the eerie blue glow of Cherenkov radiation in the water pool of a nuclear reactor, presenting it as a kind of optical sonic boom.
Write a vivid description of a ferrofluid, a dark liquid laden with magnetic nanoparticles, rising into a crown of spikes when a magnet is brought near.
Explain Gilbert Ryle's notion of a category mistake through his story of a visitor who tours Oxford's colleges, libraries and laboratories and then asks, 'But where is the University?'
Explain the scaling laws that link an animal's size to its metabolism and lifespan, including the striking observation that mice and elephants live for a roughly similar number of heartbeats.
Explain why a single quark can never be isolated, describing how pulling two quarks apart stretches the strong force like an elastic band until it snaps and the energy creates new quarks.
Explain the 'Oh-My-God particle' detected over Utah in 1991, a single subatomic cosmic ray carrying roughly the energy of a well-thrown baseball, and why its origin remains a mystery.
Explain the butterfly effect through Edward Lorenz's discovery in 1961 that rounding a number from six decimal places to three in his weather simulation produced a completely different forecast.
Argue whether fish feel pain, drawing on their nervous systems and behaviour, and what the answer would mean for how we catch and farm them.

Explain the once-dominant phlogiston theory of burning and how Antoine Lavoisier's meticulous weighing of metals and gases revealed that combustion is a combination with oxygen, helping to launch modern chemistry.

Explain Charles Darwin's late-life fascination with earthworms and his finding that their slow, ceaseless digestion builds topsoil and gradually buries ancient stones and ruins, in prose that finally gives these humble creatures their due.

Explain how the mathematics of convergent infinite series answers Zeno's paradox of Achilles and the tortoise, while acknowledging what still feels philosophically uneasy about completing infinitely many steps.

Describe the clatter and rhythm of an early nineteenth-century Jacquard loom in a Lyon silk workshop, where chains of punched cards told the threads which pattern to weave, and hint at how those cards became ancestors of computer programs.
Explain cable bacteria, which link thousands of cells end to end into centimeter-long living wires that carry electric current through seafloor mud.
Explain how Ole Rømer, timing the eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io in the 1670s, realized that light does not travel instantaneously and made the first estimate of its speed.
Compare Aristotle's notion of potential infinity with Cantor's actual, completed infinity, explaining why the shift from one to the other was among the great turning points in mathematical thought.
Describe what it would be like to spend a morning in Thoreau's cabin at Walden Pond, living deliberately and stripping life down to its essentials, in calm, unhurried prose.
Explain curves of constant width such as the Reuleaux triangle, and how they account for both the safety of round manhole covers and drill bits that can cut almost perfectly square holes.
Write a short, playful story about the 1845 experiment in the Netherlands in which trumpeters on a moving train held a steady note while musicians on the platform judged how its pitch changed.

Explain how al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century book on 'completion and balancing,' written in Baghdad's House of Wisdom, gave us the word algebra, and how he solved equations entirely in words and geometric pictures without any symbols.
Explain Hume's is-ought problem, the observation that no pile of facts about how the world is can by itself tell us how it ought to be, using an everyday example.
Write a brief, gentle story retelling the Buddhist parable of Kisa Gotami, a grieving mother sent to collect a mustard seed from a household that has never known death.

Explain survivorship bias through the story of statistician Abraham Wald, who advised that returning Second World War bombers be armored not where they were riddled with bullet holes but where they had none.
Explain how the rabies virus travels along nerves to the brain and alters its host's behaviour, making the animal aggressive and unable to swallow in ways that help the virus spread.
Describe a desert superbloom, when a rare wet winter causes seeds that have waited for years to carpet barren hills with wildflowers almost overnight.
Explain why it is nearly impossible to tickle yourself, drawing on the brain's efference copy and its habit of predicting the sensory consequences of your own movements.
Describe a resurrection plant that has lain brown, curled and seemingly dead for months coming back to green life within hours of rain.
Write a short reflective passage about Isaac Newton's time at Woolsthorpe Manor during the plague years of 1665–66, his 'years of wonder,' and the famous apple that may or may not have fallen.
Explain why a spinning top or gyroscope does not topple over, but instead swings slowly around in the motion called precession.
Explain how the bacterium Wolbachia manipulates the reproduction of the insects it infects, from killing male embryos to turning males into females, and how it is now used to block dengue.

Explain why a well-shuffled deck of 52 cards is almost certainly in an order that has never existed before in the history of the universe, and why mathematicians concluded that about seven riffle shuffles are needed to truly randomize it.
Write a brief, parable-like story illustrating Chesterton's fence, in which an eager reformer finds a gate across a country road and wants to tear it down without first learning why it was built.

Explain how the Fresnel lens, built from concentric rings of glass prisms, allowed a single lamp in a nineteenth-century lighthouse to throw a beam visible twenty miles out to sea, in prose that honours the lens as much as the light.
Explain proof by mathematical induction using an endless row of falling dominoes, and show how a finite argument can establish a truth about infinitely many numbers at once.

Describe an imaginative journey of counting past infinity through Cantor's ordinal numbers—omega, omega plus one, omega times two, omega squared, and beyond—capturing the vertigo of always finding another horizon.

Explain what is really happening when leaves turn gold and crimson in autumn, from chlorophyll breaking down to reveal yellow pigments that were there all along to the fresh reds some trees manufacture, written as a reflection on letting go.
Write a short reflective passage from the perspective of a traffic light at an empty intersection at three in the morning, faithfully cycling through green, amber and red for no one at all.
Explain prions, misfolded proteins that can corrupt their normal counterparts and cause fatal brain diseases such as kuru, which spread through funeral customs in Papua New Guinea.
Explain how a tiny anomaly in Mercury's orbit led nineteenth-century astronomers to hunt for a hidden planet called Vulcan, and how general relativity finally explained the anomaly without it.
Argue, as persuasively as you can to a stubborn skeptic, that 0.999... with its nines repeating forever is exactly equal to 1 and not merely very close to it.
Explain how Huffman coding compresses text by giving common letters short codes and rare letters long ones, drawing a parallel with the way Morse code made the frequent letter 'E' a single dot.
Describe the moment a stranger sits down at a battered public piano in a busy train station and begins to play, and how the hurrying crowd slowly changes its pace around the music.

Write a vivid narrative about the Archimedes Palimpsest, a lost treatise scraped off and overwritten as a medieval prayer book, and the modern imaging techniques that coaxed Archimedes' faded diagrams back into view.

Explain how the QWERTY keyboard layout, shaped by the mechanical quirks of nineteenth-century typewriters, became so entrenched that we still type on it long after those quirks vanished, as a gentle reflection on how accidents harden into traditions.
Describe the experience of hearing a Balinese gamelan, with its interlocking bronze patterns and paired instruments deliberately tuned slightly apart so that the whole ensemble seems to shimmer.
Explain how a giant redwood lifts water more than a hundred meters from its roots to its crown without any pump, through the cohesion-tension mechanism of transpiration.

Explain Ken Thompson's 'Reflections on Trusting Trust,' which showed how a compiler could be secretly taught to plant a backdoor in programs, and even in future copies of itself, leaving no trace in any source code anyone could inspect.
Write a vivid description of the Babylonian clay tablet known as Plimpton 322, imagining the scribe who pressed its columns of Pythagorean triples into wet clay nearly four thousand years ago.
Write a lyrical passage about the experiments in which a pulse of light was slowed to the speed of a bicycle, and then brought briefly to a complete stop, inside an ultracold cloud of atoms.

Explain, in a tone sympathetic to his reasoning, how Lord Kelvin calculated in the nineteenth century that Earth could be no more than about a hundred million years old, and why his confident estimate turned out to be far too young.
Explain, in a playful puzzle-solving tone, why a mirror seems to reverse left and right but not up and down, and what it really reverses.

Explain the 'Proust effect', how a smell such as a madeleine dipped in tea can summon a forgotten childhood with sudden intensity, describing the unusually short route from the nose to the brain's centres of memory and emotion.
Describe a walk through a memory palace, showing how the ancient method of loci lets a person recall a long list by placing vivid, absurd images along a familiar route through their childhood home.

Write a reflective passage in the spirit of Seneca's essay On the Shortness of Life, suggesting that life is long enough if we stop squandering it, beginning with a busy person who suddenly realizes it is already evening.
Argue whether it can be right to forgive someone who has never apologized or shown remorse, or whether such forgiveness quietly condones the wrong.

Explain how revolutionary France set out to define the metre as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and how Delambre and Méchain's seven-year survey concealed a small error that Méchain secretly agonized over until his death.

Explain the 'doorway effect', the frustrating experience of walking into a room and instantly forgetting why you came, and how the brain's habit of dividing experience into separate episodes may be to blame.

Explain how Alonzo Church's lambda calculus builds all of computation, including numbers, arithmetic and logic, out of nothing but functions applied to other functions, and why this austere idea quietly underlies modern programming languages.
Explain how dust blown from a dried lakebed in the Sahara crosses the Atlantic and helps fertilize the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus.

Explain Shamir's secret sharing, which splits a secret among several people so that any three together can recover it while any two learn absolutely nothing, using the geometric intuition that it takes enough points to pin down a curve.

Write a vivid passage describing the slow crushing of Ernest Shackleton's ship Endurance by Antarctic pack ice in 1915, from the groaning of her timbers to the moment the crew stood on the floe and watched her go.
Write a lyrical description of red sprites, blue jets and elves, the fleeting electrical phenomena that flicker high above thunderstorms and were not captured on camera until 1989.
Explain the Higgs field and how it gives elementary particles their mass, using the analogy of a celebrity trying to cross a crowded room at a party.
Compare the Bayesian and frequentist interpretations of probability, using the question 'what is the chance it will rain tomorrow?' to show how each school would understand the answer.

Explain what the case of patient H.M., who lost the ability to form new memories after surgery removed much of his hippocampus yet still improved at tracing a star in a mirror, taught scientists about the different kinds of memory.

Describe, as a slow-building and suspenseful scene, the morning a rumor turns into a bank run, showing how each depositor's fear of what the others will do becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy that can topple a perfectly sound bank.
Explain what scientists do and do not know about ball lightning, the glowing spheres reported to drift through rooms during thunderstorms, which have resisted a convincing explanation for centuries.
Explain why there are exactly five Platonic solids and no more, and how this small, perfect family of shapes captivated thinkers from Plato, who matched them to the elements, to Kepler.

Explain the Kula ring of the Trobriand Islands, in which shell necklaces and armbands circulate endlessly in opposite directions around a ring of islands, and what it taught anthropologists about gift exchange and prestige.

Explain the Zeigarnik effect, the tendency for unfinished tasks to nag at the mind more than completed ones, starting from the story of a waiter who remembered unpaid orders perfectly but forgot them the moment the bill was settled.

Explain why a moving bicycle stays upright, including the surprising fact that the full explanation is still debated and that neither gyroscopic effects nor steering geometry alone can account for it.

Write a brief story in which a clever student, told that there will be a surprise exam on some day next week, proves to herself that such an exam is logically impossible—until the teacher hands out the papers on Wednesday.

Write a warm descriptive passage about the Vindolanda tablets, wafer-thin wooden letters found near Hadrian's Wall, focusing on the birthday party invitation that Claudia Severa sent to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina around 100 CE.
Describe the moment in 1974 when farmers digging a well near Xi'an struck fragments of baked clay, and the silent ranks of the First Emperor's Terracotta Army began to emerge from the earth.
Explain the 'whale pump,' in which whales feeding at depth and defecating near the surface fertilize phytoplankton and help regulate the ocean's carbon cycle.

Argue whether governments should use default options, such as opt-out organ donation or automatic pension enrollment, to nudge people toward better choices, or whether such choice architecture amounts to quiet manipulation.
Argue whether a carefully tended human landscape, such as Japan's satoyama of rice paddies, coppiced woods and village streams, can be as valuable and beautiful as untouched wilderness.
Write a brief story in which one hundred prisoners, facing a perilous game of opening boxes to find their own numbers, are saved by one prisoner's insight about following the cycles of a permutation.
Explain mental accounting using the example of a theatergoer who loses a ticket and refuses to buy another, yet would happily buy one after losing the same amount of cash on the way to the show.
Argue whether the Stanford marshmallow test really measured children's willpower, or whether a child's decision to eat the treat early was a rational response to an unreliable world.
Explain how James Lind's 1747 experiment aboard HMS Salisbury, giving sailors with scurvy different remedies including oranges and lemons, became one of the first controlled clinical trials.
Explain how the discovery that most stomach ulcers are caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori overturned medical dogma, including the doctor who drank a culture of the bacteria to prove it.
Write a lyrical description of synchronous fireflies in the Great Smoky Mountains, as thousands of insects begin flashing in unison, and hint at how such synchrony arises without any leader.
Explain the density wave theory of spiral galaxies, showing why spiral arms behave more like traffic jams that stars drift through than fixed structures that would otherwise wind tighter and tighter.
Write a reflective passage about a house key kept on a keyring for years after the house it opened was demolished, an object that still fits a lock that no longer exists anywhere but in memory.

Write a brief story in which a time traveler hands a young composer the score of a famous symphony, which the composer then publishes as their own, so that no one ever actually wrote it, illustrating the bootstrap paradox.
Explain the peak-end rule, drawing on the colonoscopy study in which adding a few extra minutes of milder discomfort made patients remember the whole procedure as less unpleasant.

Argue whether it was ethical that cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 without her knowledge became one of the most important tools in medical research, and what that history should teach us about consent.
Explain how Malcom McLean's plain steel shipping container, first put to sea in 1956, quietly transformed global trade, reshaped port cities and lowered the cost of nearly everything we buy.
Explain how salmon find their way from the open ocean back to the exact stream where they hatched, guided by the Earth's magnetic field and a remembered smell, written as an elegy for homecoming.

Explain how the Moon is drifting away from Earth by a few centimetres each year while tidal friction slowly lengthens our days, so that in the age of the dinosaurs a day was noticeably shorter, writing as if the Moon were a patient thief.

Explain how airborne LiDAR, firing laser pulses through the jungle canopy, has revealed sprawling networks of Maya cities, causeways and farmland in northern Guatemala, and how it has overturned estimates of how many people once lived there.
Argue that boredom, far from being a problem to be cured with a screen, is a fertile state in which the mind wanders and creativity begins, opening with the image of a long, empty summer afternoon.

Write a thoughtful passage explaining Dunbar's number, the idea that humans can maintain only around 150 stable relationships, how it was derived from primate brain size, and what it might mean for lives lived among thousands of online contacts.
Explain Kant's distinction between things as they appear to us and things as they are in themselves, using the metaphor of a pair of tinted glasses that can never be removed.

Describe what it would be like to walk across Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni after rain, when a thin film of water turns the world's largest salt flat into a mirror and the horizon vanishes between two identical skies.

Describe the world as George Berkeley saw it, a world in which to exist is to be perceived, so that a tree standing in an empty college quad continues to be only because it is always perceived by God.

Write a vivid passage about the day the internet split over whether a dress was blue and black or white and gold, using it to show how the brain guesses the color of the light before deciding the color of objects.

Explain why there are exactly seventeen distinct symmetry types for repeating wallpaper patterns, and how the tile-makers of the Alhambra seem to have explored many of them centuries before mathematicians classified them.

Describe, in an eerie and suspenseful tone, the quantum suicide thought experiment, in which an experimenter sits before a device triggered by quantum events and, if the many-worlds interpretation is true, seems never to experience their own death.

Using the image of a radio tuner, explain the cocktail party effect: how your attention can lock onto a single conversation in a roaring room yet still snap toward the sound of your own name spoken across it.

Write a meditative passage on the Hebrew word 'hevel' in Ecclesiastes, usually translated as vanity but literally meaning vapor or breath, and what it means to see human striving as mist on a cold morning.

Explain the Poincaré conjecture in plain language, using the image of a lasso that can always be slipped off a ball but not off a doughnut, and why its proof in the early 2000s was hailed as a landmark of topology.

Explain, in a tone of quiet wonder, how Eratosthenes estimated the circumference of the Earth around 240 BCE using only the noon shadow of a stick in Alexandria, reports of a sunlit well at Syene, and the distance between the two cities.

Explain how the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which struck on the morning of All Saints' Day while the churches were full, shook not only a great city but the Enlightenment's comfortable belief that this is the best of all possible worlds.

Explain how researchers are now reading the carbonized papyrus scrolls of Herculaneum, charred by Vesuvius in 79 CE and far too fragile to open, by combining X-ray scans with machine learning that detects faint traces of ancient ink.

Write a lyrical passage about how a single smell, such as a grandmother's kitchen or sun-warmed pine, can unlock a vivid memory instantly, touching on the direct wiring between the nose and the brain's memory centers.
Argue whether string theory, after decades without a single confirmed experimental prediction, still deserves to be called science.

Write a brief, playful story narrated by the sheep who, along with a duck and a rooster, became one of the first passengers of a Montgolfier hot-air balloon before King Louis XVI at Versailles in 1783.
Explain the hypothesis that it rains diamonds deep inside Neptune and Uranus, where crushing pressures squeeze carbon out of methane into crystals that sink toward the core.
Explain how Earth's magnetic field is generated by its churning molten core, and how magnetic 'stripes' frozen into the rocks of the seafloor show that the field has flipped many times.
Explain how cane toads, introduced to Australia in 1935 to control beetles, became one of the continent's most notorious invaders and even evolved longer legs at the advancing front.
Write a short reflective passage about the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon, the uncanny sense that a word, car model or song you have just learned about is suddenly appearing everywhere.
Explain Mencius' argument that anyone who suddenly sees a toddler about to fall into a well feels alarm and compassion, and why he took this instant reaction as evidence that human nature is good.
Describe the thought experiment a sixteen-year-old Albert Einstein imagined, of racing alongside a beam of light, and how that daydream grew into a revolution in our understanding of space and time.
Describe the end of the cosmic dark ages, when the first enormous, short-lived stars ignited in a universe that had never known starlight.

Explain the Capgras delusion, in which a person becomes convinced that a loved one has been replaced by an identical impostor, and how a broken link between face recognition and emotional response might produce it.
Explain the moral dilemma facing Arjuna on the battlefield of Kurukshetra in the Bhagavad Gita and Krishna's teaching that one should act without attachment to the fruits of action.

Explain Thomas Hobbes' state of nature, in which life without government would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short,' and why he thought rational people would trade freedom for a sovereign's protection.

Write a lyrical description of October 1957, when people around the world huddled over shortwave radios to hear the faint beep-beep of Sputnik passing overhead, the first sign that humanity had placed a new star in the sky.
Explain why the naked mole rat is one of biology's strangest mammals, living in queen-ruled colonies like insects, resisting cancer and surviving many minutes without oxygen.

Explain the dining philosophers problem, in which five thinkers sharing five forks around a table can all starve if each grabs the fork on their left at once, as a way of illustrating deadlock in computer systems.
Explain the curious case of Bir Tawil, a patch of desert between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims, and how two conflicting border lines left it one of the last unclaimed places on Earth.

Explain the philosophical significance of Augustine's confession that as a teenager he stole pears he did not even want, purely for the thrill of doing what was forbidden, and what it reveals about the nature of wrongdoing.

Explain, in the voice of a patient museum guide, why the popular belief that medieval Europeans thought the Earth was flat is itself a myth, and how this misconception was largely invented in the nineteenth century.

Write a short passage explaining what Gregor Mendel discovered by crossing thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden, and why his laws of inheritance lay ignored for more than three decades before three scientists rediscovered them almost simultaneously in 1900.

Write a brief story about Thales of Miletus, mocked for falling into a well while gazing at the stars, who uses his knowledge of the heavens to corner the market on olive presses and prove that philosophers could be rich if they wished.
Argue whether the multiverse can count as a legitimate scientific idea if no other universe can ever be observed.

Explain the idea of a ring species using the greenish warblers that encircle the Tibetan Plateau, where neighboring populations interbreed but the two ends of the ring no longer recognize each other as mates.

Describe the MONIAC, a 1949 analog computer in which colored water flowing through tanks and pipes modeled a national economy, capturing the strange beauty of watching taxes, savings and spending literally pour from one chamber to another.

Explain why ancient glacier ice glows a deep, almost electric blue, describing how centuries of compression squeeze out the air bubbles and let the ice absorb the red end of the spectrum, in prose that evokes standing inside an ice cave.
Explain the Great Oxidation Event, when oxygen released by cyanobacteria poisoned much of early life and permanently transformed Earth's atmosphere, oceans and rocks.
Describe the controlled chaos of an open-outcry trading pit at a commodities exchange the moment the opening bell rings, with its shouting traders, brightly colored jackets and frantic hand signals.

Explain how dendrochronologists read tree rings as a diary of past droughts, fires and cold summers, written so that the cross-section of a fallen oak feels like an old book being opened for the first time.
Explain Gilbert Ryle's distinction between knowing how and knowing that, using the example of someone who rides a bicycle flawlessly but could never state the physics that keeps them upright.
Compare Batesian and Müllerian mimicry, using harmless hoverflies dressed as wasps and toxic butterflies that share the same warning colors, and explain why each strategy pays off.

Write a brief story in which a nineteenth-century astronomer notices that the early pages of his book of logarithm tables are far more worn than the later ones, and slowly realizes what this reveals about the numbers of the world.
